title: Depression
about: Depression is more than a few days of sadness — it is a treatable illness where low mood, loss of interest and low energy persist for weeks and get in the way of daily life. It is common in South Africa and highly treatable.
signs: Feeling down, hopeless or empty most of the day, nearly every day, for more than two weeks
Losing interest or pleasure in things usually enjoyed
Tiredness and low energy even after rest
Sleeping far more or far less than usual; waking in the early hours
Appetite and weight changes
Difficulty concentrating or making decisions
Feeling worthless or excessive guilt
Moving or speaking noticeably slower, or being restless and agitated
Thoughts that life is not worth living — these need urgent attention
selfHelpStrategies: Keep moving: 30 minutes of walking most days has real antidepressant effect
Keep connected: one small daily contact with a trusted person protects against isolation
Keep a routine: getting up, dressing and doing one small task each day rebuilds structure
Sunlight and outside time in the morning help reset sleep
Limit alcohol — it is a depressant and worsens mood and sleep
Break tasks into small steps and celebrate small wins; depression shrinks what feels possible
whenToGetProfessionalHelp: Seek help at the local clinic if low mood or loss of interest lasts more than two weeks, affects work, home or study, or brings any thought of self-harm. Depression is treated every day at primary healthcare level in South Africa — counselling, medication or both. Help urgently the same day if there are thoughts of suicide.
saResources: SADAG (South African Depression and Anxiety Group) helpline: 0800 567 567 — free counselling and referrals
Lifeline South Africa: 0861 322 322 — 24-hour crisis counselling
Nearest public clinic: ask for a mental health consultation; treatment is free in the public sector
Emergency: 10177 (ambulance) or 112 from a cellphone

source.authority: WHO / SA NDoH Mental Health Policy Framework / SADAG

title: Anxiety
about: Anxiety becomes a problem when persistent worry, tension or physical symptoms like a racing heart last for months and interfere with work, relationships or sleep. It is among the most common mental health conditions and responds well to treatment.
signs: Excessive worry most days for six months or more, difficult to control
Restlessness, feeling on edge or irritable
Muscle tension, headaches, jaw clenching
Tiredness and poor sleep, especially trouble falling asleep
Difficulty concentrating; mind going blank
Stomach upset, loose stools or nausea linked to stress
Avoiding places, tasks or people that trigger the worry
selfHelpStrategies: Slow breathing: in for 4 counts, out for 6 counts, for five minutes — calms the body's alarm system
Limit caffeine and energy drinks — they copy and amplify anxiety symptoms
Worry time: write worries down once a day at a set time rather than carrying them all day
Regular exercise reduces baseline anxiety over weeks
Reduce alcohol and nicotine — both worsen anxiety after the short relief wears off
Stay in the present: name five things that can be seen, four heard, three felt
whenToGetProfessionalHelp: Book a clinic visit if worry or physical symptoms last for months, cause avoidance of daily life, or come with panic attacks, low mood or drinking to cope. Counselling and, where needed, medication are available at public clinics; persistent anxiety is not a character flaw or something to simply push through.
saResources: SADAG helpline: 0800 567 567
Lifeline South Africa: 0861 322 322
Nearest public clinic — ask about mental health services or a referral

source.authority: WHO / SA NDoH Mental Health Policy Framework / SADAG

title: Panic Attacks
about: A panic attack is a sudden rush of intense fear with strong physical symptoms — racing heart, breathlessness, dizziness — usually peaking within ten minutes. It feels dangerous but is not physically harmful, and panic disorder is treatable.
signs: Sudden pounding heart, sweating, trembling
Breathlessness or a feeling of choking
Chest tightness, dizziness or feeling faint
Tingling hands or feet, numbness
Fear of losing control, going crazy or dying
Worry for weeks afterwards about having another attack, or avoiding places where one happened
selfHelpStrategies: Remember: panic peaks and passes in minutes — it cannot harm the body even though it feels overwhelming
Breathe slowly: in for 4, out for 6; longer out-breath switches off the alarm
Ground yourself: press both feet into the floor, name five things that can be seen
Do not flee the place if it is safe to stay — leaving teaches the brain the place was dangerous
Cut caffeine, energy drinks and nicotine, which trigger attacks in sensitive people
whenToGetProfessionalHelp: A first panic attack should be checked at a clinic to rule out physical causes such as heart, thyroid or breathing problems. Return promptly if attacks recur, if worry about attacks limits daily life, or if chest pain is severe, lasts long, or comes with sweating and nausea — treat that as a possible heart emergency (call 10177).
saResources: SADAG helpline: 0800 567 567
Emergency: 10177 for suspected heart emergency
Nearest public clinic for assessment and counselling referral

title: Post-Traumatic Stress (PTSD)
about: After experiencing or witnessing violence, a crash, disaster or assault, some people develop post-traumatic stress: the event stays 'live' in the mind and body for months. In South Africa, where trauma exposure is high, effective treatment exists and asking for it is strength, not weakness.
signs: Re-experiencing: unwanted memories, nightmares or flashbacks of the event
Avoidance of reminders — places, people, conversations, thoughts
Feeling constantly on guard: jumpiness, irritability, easily startled, trouble sleeping
Numbness: feeling cut off from others, flattened emotions
Strong guilt, shame or anger connected to the event
Symptoms lasting more than a month and disrupting work, home or relationships
selfHelpStrategies: Rhythm and routine: regular sleep, meals and gentle exercise steady the nervous system
Tell one trusted person what happened — silence feeds trauma
Limit alcohol — it numbs at first but deepens sleep problems, nightmares and anxiety
Learn grounding for flashbacks: stamp feet, hold something cold, name the current year and place
Return to meaningful activities step by step, at a pace that feels manageable
whenToGetProfessionalHelp: Seek trauma counselling if symptoms last beyond a month, worsen, or make home or work impossible. Psychological therapy for PTSD is effective and available through clinics, trauma centres and NGOs. Urgent help is needed if there are thoughts of suicide, dangerous drinking, or violence at home.
saResources: SADAG helpline: 0800 567 567 — also offers PTSD support and referrals
Lifeline South Africa: 0861 322 322 — 24-hour crisis and trauma counselling
GBV Command Centre: 0800 428 428 (24 hours) or Please Call Me *120*7867# — for abuse and violence support
Rape Crisis and provincial Thuthuzela Care Centres — care, counselling and medico-legal support after sexual assault; police stations and hospitals can direct

source.authority: WHO / SA NDoH Mental Health Policy Framework / SADAG

title: Grief and Loss
about: Grief is the natural response to losing a loved one, a job, a relationship or health. There is no correct timetable, but support helps people move through it rather than getting stuck in it.
signs: Waves of sadness, crying, or numbness that come and go
Difficulty believing the loss is real
Sleep and appetite changes
Irritability, guilt or anger, including anger at the person who died
Withdrawal from usual activities and people
Physical tiredness and aches; feeling that meaning has drained out of daily life
selfHelpStrategies: Let grief come in waves — setbacks on hard days such as anniversaries are normal, not failure
Talk about the person who died with people who knew them; share stories rather than avoiding the name
Keep basics going: eat something at usual mealtimes, keep a sleep routine, walk daily
Accept practical help; grief is not carried better alone
Cultural, religious and traditional mourning practices give many people structure — use what is familiar and comforting
whenToGetProfessionalHelp: Consider clinic or counselling support if grief is still preventing eating, sleeping or working months later, if there is heavy drinking to cope, or if thoughts of joining the person who died appear — that is a warning sign needing urgent support. Counselling also helps when grief is complicated by a sudden, violent or stigmatised death.
saResources: SADAG helpline: 0800 567 567
Lifeline South Africa: 0861 322 322
Faith and community leaders and traditional structures offer widely used mourning support
Hospice and palliative-care services in many districts offer bereavement counselling

title: Harmful Alcohol Use
about: Alcohol harms health, safety and family life even before dependence develops — South Africa has among the highest risky drinking levels in the world. The good news: cutting down works, and treatment is free in the public sector.
signs: Drinking more or longer than intended
Failed attempts to cut down
Craving alcohol; spending much of the day drinking or recovering from it
Work, study or family problems caused by drinking
Drinking in situations that are dangerous, such as before driving
Needing more alcohol for the same effect; shakes, sweating or anxiety when stopping — signs of physical dependence
Continuing to drink despite clear harm to health or relationships
selfHelpStrategies: Count the drinks for one week — most people underestimate
Set limits before drinking occasions and alternate every drink with water
Have at least three alcohol-free days each week
Avoid drinking to cope with stress, grief or insomnia — it worsens all three
Tell one trusted person the plan; accountability doubles success
Never drink and drive, and never drink during pregnancy — no amount is safe for the unborn baby
whenToGetProfessionalHelp: Seek help at the clinic if drinking is harming health, work or family, or if stopping causes shaking, sweating, seeing things or fits — stopping heavy long-term drinking suddenly can be dangerous and is best done with medical support. Treatment programmes, detoxification and SANCA (South African National Council on Alcoholism and Drug Dependence) services are available.
saResources: SANCA (South African National Council on Alcoholism and Drug Dependence) — outpatient and inpatient programmes; the nearest centre can be found via clinics or sanca.org.za
SADAG helpline: 0800 567 567 — also runs substance-use support and referrals
Lifeline South Africa: 0861 322 322
Public clinics and district hospitals — detoxification and referral are free

title: Substance Use — tik, whoonga, cannabis and other drugs
about: Stimulants like tik (crystal methamphetamine), opioids like whoonga (heroin-based), and cannabis cause serious health and social harm. Substance use disorder is a medical condition, not a moral failure — and treatment works.
signs: Strong craving and loss of control over how much or how often the drug is used
Neglecting work, school, family or self-care
Money, belongings or household goods going missing; new debt
Sudden weight loss, poor sleep, decaying teeth (tik), or drowsiness and pinpoint pupils (opioids)
New social circle, secrecy, hostility when the drug is mentioned
Withdrawal when stopping: depression and crashes (tik), flu-like pain and craving (opioids), irritability (cannabis)
Continuing despite arrest, illness, overdose or family breakdown
selfHelpStrategies: Name one reason to stop that is personally bigger than the high — a child, a job, a dream — and write it where it is seen daily
Break ties with using situations and connections wherever possible; recovery is easier with distance
Replace, do not just remove: exercise, faith structures, work or study fill the hours the drug filled
Do not try to quit opioids alone — Medication-Assisted Treatment is available and reduces overdose and relapse
If someone overdoses on opioids: keep them awake, on their side, and call 10177 immediately
whenToGetProfessionalHelp: Seek treatment at the clinic, or via SANCA, if drug use is harming health or family, if quitting alone keeps failing, or if there is any overdose. Anyone injecting drugs can access needle services and HIV prevention; anyone using drugs can access HIV testing. Treatment programmes, social workers and support groups exist in all provinces.
saResources: SANCA — the national network of substance-use treatment centres; the nearest centre can be found via clinics or sanca.org.za
SADAG helpline: 0800 567 567 — substance-use support and referrals
Public clinics: HIV testing, TB screening and referral are free and judgement-free
Overdose emergency: 10177

title: Suicide Risk — Warning Signs and What to Do
about: Suicide is a leading cause of death in young South Africans, and most people who attempt it give warning signs. Knowing the signs and asking directly saves lives. Asking about suicide does not plant the idea — it opens the door to help.
signs: Talking about death, dying, being a burden, or wanting to disappear
Saying goodbye, giving away treasured possessions, or putting affairs in order
Withdrawing from friends, family and activities
Sudden calm or apparent 'peace' after a period of despair
Hopelessness: saying nothing will ever change or get better
Increased drinking or drug use; recklessness
Previous suicide attempt — the strongest single warning sign
Recent major loss, humiliation, violence or crisis
selfHelpStrategies: Ask directly and calmly: 'Are you thinking about suicide?' — direct questions invite honest answers
Listen without argument, shock or lectures; do not promise secrecy about a life at risk
Remove or distance the means where possible — medicines, pesticides, firearms, rope
Do not leave the person alone; stay, or arrange for someone trusted to stay
Get professional help the same day: clinic, crisis line, hospital; go together if possible
For anyone having these thoughts: suicidal thoughts are a symptom that passes with the right help — reach out to one person today; the crisis lines below are free and staffed by trained counsellors
whenToGetProfessionalHelp: Treat any suicide plan, preparation or act as an emergency: go to the nearest clinic or hospital, or call 10177. After any attempt, hospital care is essential. Ongoing support afterwards — counselling, clinic follow-up, family involvement — saves lives.
saResources: SADAG suicide crisis helpline: 0800 567 567 — free, and can talk through the situation step by step
Lifeline South Africa: 0861 322 322 — 24-hour crisis counselling
Emergency: 10177 (ambulance) or 112 from a cellphone
Nearest clinic or hospital emergency department — same-day assessment

title: Self-Harm
about: Self-harm — cutting, burning or otherwise injuring oneself — is usually a way of coping with overwhelming emotional pain, not attention-seeking. It needs a caring response and support to learn safer ways of coping.
signs: Unexplained cuts, burns or bruises, often on arms or thighs, explained as 'accidents'
Wearing long sleeves or covering up regardless of heat
Blood-stained tissues or clothing, hidden sharp objects
Emotional swings, self-criticism, or deep shame after injuries
Withdrawal and isolation
selfHelpStrategies: Delay and substitute: when the urge comes, wait ten minutes and use intense sensation that is not damaging — an ice cube in the hand, a rubber band snap, hard exercise
Name and rate the feeling out of ten — self-harm often happens when feeling is unbearable and unspoken
Tell one trusted adult or friend; secrecy deepens the pattern
Care for wounds properly: clean water, clean dressing, clinic for any wound that will not stop bleeding, is deep, or becomes red and weeping
whenToGetProfessionalHelp: Book clinic support as soon as the pattern is recognised — self-harm is treatable, and therapy builds safer coping. Seek urgent care for deep wounds, burns, or overdose, and treat any mention of suicide with the seriousness in mh-008.
saResources: SADAG helpline: 0800 567 567 — includes support for self-harm
Lifeline South Africa: 0861 322 322
Childline South Africa: 116 — free, 24-hour line for children and teens
Emergency: 10177

title: Bipolar Disorder
about: Bipolar disorder involves episodes of depression and episodes of mania — abnormally high energy, mood or irritability lasting days. It is a lifelong condition that, with treatment and routine, allows a full and stable life.
signs: Depressive episodes as in mh-001
Manic episodes: days of high energy, little need for sleep, racing thoughts and rapid speech
Inflated confidence or grand plans; impulsive spending, risky behaviour or decisions
Irritability when challenged during a high period
Episodes severe enough to damage work, study, money or relationships
Sometimes psychosis during severe episodes
selfHelpStrategies: Learn personal early warning signs of both highs and lows, and share them with a trusted person
Protect sleep fiercely — losing sleep is the most common trigger for mania
Take mood-stabilising medicine exactly as prescribed; stopping during wellness is what usually causes relapse
Keep a simple daily mood log to spot drift early
Avoid alcohol and recreational drugs — they destabilise mood
whenToGetProfessionalHelp: Seek assessment at a clinic if mood swings are extreme or damaging. Urgent care is needed for mania with reckless spending or risky behaviour, refusal to eat or sleep, any psychosis, or thoughts of suicide — go to the hospital or call 10177. Long-term care usually involves referral to mental health services.
saResources: SADAG helpline: 0800 567 567 — includes bipolar support groups
Lifeline South Africa: 0861 322 322
Public clinics and district hospitals — assessment, referral and free treatment
Emergency: 10177

source.authority: WHO / SA NDoH Mental Health Policy Framework / SADAG

title: Schizophrenia and Psychosis
about: Psychosis means losing touch with shared reality — hearing voices or holding beliefs others do not share. Schizophrenia is the best-known psychotic illness. With treatment, many people with psychosis live and work in their communities; family understanding makes a big difference.
signs: Hearing voices or seeing things others do not, often distressing
Strongly held beliefs that others find clearly false — of being followed, poisoned or specially chosen
Disorganised speech or behaviour; difficulty following conversation
Social withdrawal and loss of interest or function over months
Neglecting self-care, hygiene or safety
Family and cultural context matters: what matters is distress and loss of function
selfHelpStrategies: For families: stay calm, do not argue with the beliefs or mock them; short, clear sentences work best
Reduce stimulation during episodes — noise, crowds and confrontation worsen symptoms
Support medicine-taking quietly and consistently; relapse most often follows stopping treatment
Keep a record of early warning signs and who to call
Do not try to restrain someone who is frightened unless there is immediate danger — clear space and call for help
whenToGetProfessionalHelp: Arrange assessment at the clinic for any suspected psychosis — early treatment improves outcomes dramatically. Urgent help (clinic, hospital or 10177) is needed for danger to self or others, refusal of food or drink, or total self-neglect. Community mental health services follow up patients at home in many districts.
saResources: Nearest clinic — mental health services and referral to district mental health teams
SADAG helpline: 0800 567 567 — guidance for families
Cape Mental Health, Comcare and other provincial NGOs support families (find via clinic or SADAG referrals)
Emergency: 10177

source.authority: WHO / SA NDoH Mental Health Policy Framework

title: Stress and Burnout
about: Everyday stress becomes burnout when long-term pressure — work, unemployment, debt, caregiving — drains energy, hope and the ability to cope. Burnout is a signal to change the load, not a personal weakness.
signs: Exhaustion not relieved by rest
Feeling cynical, detached or numb about work or responsibilities
Falling performance, forgetfulness and difficulty concentrating
Physical complaints: headaches, tense neck and shoulders, stomach upset, frequent colds
Short temper or tears close to the surface
Relying on alcohol, tobacco or other substances to get through
selfHelpStrategies: Protect sleep first — it is the foundation of stress tolerance
One true break a day, even twenty minutes of walking, music or quiet
Sort worries into 'can act on' and 'cannot control' lists; act on one small item from the first list
Say no to one non-essential commitment a week
Move the body daily — exercise is one of the most effective stress treatments available
Talk to someone trusted regularly — carrying stress alone multiplies it
whenToGetProfessionalHelp: Seek clinic support if stress is causing ongoing insomnia, depression or anxiety symptoms, heavy substance use, or constant physical illness — or if there are chest pains, which always need a medical check. Social workers at clinics can also assist with applications and support for money and family stressors.
saResources: SADAG helpline: 0800 567 567
Lifeline South Africa: 0861 322 322
Clinic social worker services — free

title: Mental Health in Teenagers
about: Half of mental illness begins before age 18. Teenagers often show distress through behaviour — irritability, school decline, withdrawal — rather than saying they feel depressed. Adults who notice early and respond calmly change the course of a young life.
signs: Two or more weeks of low mood, irritability or tearfulness
Falling marks or school refusal
Withdrawal from friends and activities once enjoyed
Sleeping far more or less; appetite changes
Self-harm marks or covered clothing (mh-009)
Talk of hopelessness, death or being a burden (mh-008)
New substance use or risky behaviour
Severe anxiety before tests or social situations
selfHelpStrategies: For adults: listen more than lecture — a teenager who feels judged stops talking
Ask directly about mood and even about suicide; asking protects, it does not plant ideas
Protect sleep routines and limit late-night screens together
Keep one trusted adult in the picture — a teacher, coach, aunt or uncle can be the bridge to help
Encourage exercise and keep meals regular; both stabilise mood
whenToGetProfessionalHelp: Arrange help when low mood, anxiety, behaviour change or self-harm lasts more than two weeks or affects school. Urgent help for any suicidal talk, plan or act, or any psychosis — same day, no exceptions. School-based support, clinics and NGOs all serve teenagers; consent of a parent or guardian is normally arranged, and teens can still talk to counsellors confidentially on the crisis lines.
saResources: Childline South Africa: 116 — free, 24-hour counselling for children and teens
SADAG helpline: 0800 567 567 — includes teen support and referrals
Lifeline South Africa: 0861 322 322
School counsellors and life orientation teachers can start the referral
Emergency: 10177

source.authority: WHO adolescent mental health / SADAG / Childline SA

title: South African Crisis and Support Lines Directory
about: Free crisis lines exist for exactly the moments when problems feel too heavy to carry alone. Calling is free from most networks, the lines are staffed by trained counsellors, and no problem is too small.
lines: SADAG (South African Depression and Anxiety Group): 0800 567 567 — depression, anxiety, suicidal thoughts, mental health information and referrals
Lifeline South Africa: 0861 322 322 — 24-hour crisis counselling for any crisis, including trauma and abuse
Childline South Africa: 116 — free 24-hour line for children and teenagers
GBV Command Centre: 0800 428 428 (24 hours) — gender-based violence counselling, social workers and shelter referral; Please Call Me *120*7867#; SMS 'help' to 31531
Ambulance: 10177 — medical emergencies, including overdose and suicide attempts
Poisons Information Helpline: 0861 555 777 — what to do after swallowing medicines, chemicals or paraffin
whenToGetProfessionalHelp: Call immediately when there is any risk to life, when a crisis feels unbearable, or simply when support is needed and there is no one else to talk to. For ongoing care, the nearest public clinic provides free mental health assessment, treatment and referral.
saResources: All lines above are free to call
Public clinics: free mental health services in every district
SANCA centres for substance-use treatment
SADAG website (sadag.org) lists additional support groups and resources
